title: Breakfast grace
hook: a short blessing turns a meal into thanksgiving
tomorrow: can the drive to school be a pilgrimage?

segments.voice: A week from mercy to morning: as we forgive, bear it, pray for them, then first thought, all of today, and yesterday, baptized again.

Phones come out before forks. The plate gets its photo before anyone takes a bite. There's an older pause at that same moment, and it isn't for anyone's feed. One familiar Catholic grace asks God to bless us and these gifts we're about to receive from his bounty, through Christ our Lord. A few seconds over a bowl of cereal. So why stop at all, when the food is right there?
screen: `PHONES BEFORE FORKS.` → `AN OLDER PAUSE.` → `WHY STOP AT ALL?`

segments.voice: Because in this tradition, thanks comes first, before the food is even tasted. Paul gives the reason in his first letter to Timothy: "every creature of God is good, and nothing to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving." Received with thanksgiving: that's the hinge. The same food, received as a gift instead of grabbed. The Gospels show Jesus doing it. He takes bread, gives thanks, then breaks it, for crowds on a hillside and at the Last Supper. And here's one to tell a friend over breakfast: the Catechism says the word Eucharist comes from the Greek for giving thanks. So a morning grace is a small cousin of the Mass: bread, thanks, then eating. The words can be the familiar grace, one sentence of your own, or the sign of the cross over a bowl. It's short on purpose. Look at the week's mornings together: a first thought turned to God, the whole day offered, water at the sink, and now a pause at the table. Ordinary holiness, so far, takes about a minute.
screen: `RECEIVED WITH THANKSGIVING.` · `HE GAVE THANKS, THEN BROKE IT.` · `EUCHARIST MEANS THANKSGIVING.` · `SHORT ON PURPOSE.` · then, large: `THANKS FIRST.`

segments.voice: If you have something to eat or drink nearby, take one bite or one sip, slowly, and taste it all the way through before you swallow. Before the next, pause for one breath of thanks, to God if you pray, or to everyone whose hands it passed through on its way to you.
Breakfast grace. A short blessing before the first bite that turns a meal into thanks.
Your line: thanks first. Before the photo, before the fork, before the first bite. Enjoy your breakfast.

howItsDone: Catholic families often say a short grace before meals, such as 'Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts', with the sign of the cross; some also give thanks after eating.

one sentence of thanks, or a sign of the cross over a bowl, is grace too.
the word Eucharist comes from the Greek for giving thanks
the Catechism says so: the Mass is an action of thanksgiving.

fork.setup: at a friend's house, her family dives straight into dinner without grace. you usually pause first. what fits today's idea?
options: give thanks quietly, maybe a small sign of the cross, then eat.
ask everyone to stop and pray together before anybody eats.
skip it this once; grace only counts when the whole table says it.
fork.reveal: grace is thanks first, not a performance. a silent thanks keeps the pause without asking anyone else to share it.

chat.says: last morning at Abuela's. she made me say grace and i rushed it so fast Lupe laughed. does speed-grace count?
options: It counts, but slow down one breath. The point is thanks first, before the first bite.
Only if you say the full official grace word for word. Otherwise it doesn't.
Not really. Grace is mainly for big dinners like holidays, not for breakfast.
chat.meaning: Grace puts thanks before the first bite. Paul says what's received with thanksgiving is good; even a short grace does that.

Eucharist.meaning: the Mass, and the consecrated bread and wine

Last Supper.meaning: Jesus's final meal with his disciples before his death

Catechism.meaning: the Church's official summary of what it teaches

The traditional grace is described, not quoted, in the voice ('asks God to bless us and these gifts we're about to receive from his bounty, through Christ our Lord'); howItsDone names its opening words. Confirm.

Jesus giving thanks over bread: Matthew 15:36 and Luke 22:19 use 'gave thanks'; Mark 6:41 has 'blessed'. The voice says 'gives thanks... for crowds on a hillside and at the Last Supper'; confirm the feeding reference (Matthew 15:36).
'The Catechism says the word Eucharist comes from the Greek for giving thanks' rests on CCC 1328 (eucharistein). Confirm.
'Phones come out before forks' is an illustration, not a claim about how many people do it.
